# Volume 2 — I An Irate Neighbor

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

One mature afternoon during August, a slender, lofty young woman, who was “half-past sixteen,” featuring grave gray eyes alongside locks her acquaintances labeled auburn, had taken a seat upon the wide red sandstone doorstep belonging to a farmhouse on St. Brendan’s Island, resolutely determined to translate a specific number of Virgil’s lines.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0000 }

However, a day in August during the afternoon, featuring azure mists wrapping the gathered crops on the hills, small breezes murmuring softly among the poplars, and a shimmering brilliance of crimson poppies blazing brightly in contrast to the deep thicket of small fir trees within a nook of the cherry orchard, suited dreaming far better than extinct tongues. Unregarded, the Virgil presently slid down to the grass, and Nell, resting her chin upon her joined hands, while her gaze rested on the magnificent pile of soft clouds gathering directly above Mr. J. A. Pettifer’s residence resembling a vast pale peak, found herself distant in a delightful realm in which a particular schoolmaster was achieving an extraordinary labor, moulding the fates of prospective leaders, and encouraging young intellects and souls toward noble and grand aspirations.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0001 }

Undeniably, if one reduced things to stern reality . . . a process, it has to be acknowledged, Nell rarely engaged in before it became necessary . . . the existence of much potential for famous people within Brierley school appeared improbable; yet the outcome remained uncertain when an instructor exerted her sway toward the right. Nell possessed particular optimistic visions regarding the achievements a educator could realize if she simply approached the matter correctly; and she was right in the middle of an enchanting picture, four decades in the future, wherein a celebrated figure . . . the precise nature of his renown was preserved in a handy ambiguity, though Nell felt it would be quite lovely for him to be a university president or a Canadian prime minister . . . bent deeply above her withered hand and declared to her that she was the one who had initially ignited his drive, and that the entirety of his life's achievements stemmed from the instruction she had imparted decades prior at Brierley school. This enjoyable reverie was abruptly broken by a exceedingly disagreeable disturbance.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0002 }

A modest small Jersey cow hastened down the path, and five seconds after, Mr. Pettifer made his appearance . . . provided that “arrived” is not an excessively gentle word for expressing the way he burst into the yard.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0003 }

He leaped above the fence rather than taking the time to unlatch the gate, furiously approaching a surprised Nell, who had gotten up and was observing him with a degree of confusion. The man, Mr. Pettifer, was the new neighbor living directly to their right, and she had never been introduced to him previously, despite having caught sight of him on one or two occasions.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0004 }

Prior to Nell returning from Regent’s in early April, the Abernethy place's western neighbor, Mr. Robert Bell, had disposed of his farm and relocated to Port Marlow. A individual named Mr. J. A. Pettifer purchased his property, and nothing beyond his name and his status as a New Brunswick man was recognized concerning him. Nevertheless, within a month of arriving in Brierley, he had acquired the fame of being an eccentric individual . . . “a crank,” declared Mrs. Agatha Sowerby. Mrs. Agatha was a candid woman, as those among you who might have previously met her will recall. Mr. Pettifer was undoubtedly distinct from the rest of humanity . . . and that defines the fundamental trait of a crank, as all people are aware.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0005 }

To begin with, he maintained his own home and had openly declared that no foolish women were desired near his premises. The women of Brierley avenged themselves through the macabre stories they told regarding his culinary and domestic skills. He had employed young John Henry Carter of Pale Sands, and it was John Henry who initiated the rumors. To begin with, fixed meal times were nonexistent in the Pettifer household. Mr. Pettifer “got a bite” whenever hunger struck him, and should John Henry happen to be present then, he received a portion, but should he be absent, waiting for Mr. Pettifer’s subsequent bout of hunger was his only option. John Henry sadly declared that he would have succumbed to starvation had he not returned home on Sundays to get a proper fill, and had his mother not consistently provided him with a basket of “grub” to carry back on Monday mornings.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0006 }

Regarding the chore of dishwashing, Mr. Pettifer never even pretended to perform it except when a wet Sunday occurred. On those occasions, he set to work and cleaned every one of them together inside the rainwater hogshead, after which he allowed them to dry by draining.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0007 }

Furthermore, Mr. Pettifer was “stingy.” Upon being requested to chip in for the Rev. Mr. Wace’s earnings, he replied that he would hold off to observe how many dollars’ worth of benefit he derived from his sermons initially . . . he was disinclined to purchase a pig in a poke. Furthermore, when Mrs. Sowerby paid a visit to request a donation for missions . . . and by the way to catch a glimpse of the interior of the home . . . he informed her that a greater number of pagans existed among the elderly female busybodies in Brierley than in any other location he was aware of, and he would gladly give money toward a mission aimed at converting them to Christianity if she would take it on. Mrs. Agatha departed and remarked that it was a blessing poor Mrs. Robert Bell was resting peacefully in her tomb, because witnessing the condition of her dwelling, which she once held in such high esteem, would have crushed her spirit.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0008 }

“Well, the kitchen floor was scrubbed by her every other day,” Mrs. Sowerby said to Thirza Abernethy with indignation, “and if its present state were visible to you! As I crossed it, gathering up my skirts was necessary.”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0009 }

Lastly, Mr. Pettifer possessed a parrot named Nutmeg. No one in Brierley had previously owned a parrot; as a result, the act was regarded as hardly proper. And what a bird it was! According to John Henry Carter, there had never existed a more wicked creature. Its cursing was awful. Mrs. Carter would have removed John Henry immediately had she been certain of finding him another job. Furthermore, Nutmeg had chomp-bitten a chunk directly from the rear of John Henry’s neck on an occasion when he bent over excessively close to its cage. Mrs. Carter displayed the scar to all when the unfortunate John Henry visited home on Sundays.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0010 }

Every one of these thoughts raced through Nell’s mind while Mr. Pettifer, seemingly entirely rendered mute by anger, remained standing in front of her. Even at his most pleasant, Mr. Pettifer would not have been judged a good-looking man; he was low in stature, heavy-set, and lacking hair; and at present, with his circular countenance turned violet from fury and his bulging azure eyes nearly protruding from his skull, Nell considered him truly the most repulsive individual she had ever beheld.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0011 }

Suddenly Mr. Pettifer regained the ability to speak.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0012 }

“I will not tolerate this,” he gasped out, “not for one more day, do you understand, miss. Good heavens, this makes three times, miss . . . three separate occasions! Patience isn't a virtue anymore, miss. On the previous occasion, I gave your aunt a warning that it must not happen again . . . yet she permitted it . . . she committed it . . . what is her reason for doing so, that is the question I require an answer to. That is the purpose of my visit, miss.”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0013 }

“Are you going to clarify the problem?” Nell inquired, using her utmost formal tone. Lately, she had devoted much effort to rehearsing this demeanor so it would function smoothly once the school term commenced; nevertheless, it seemed to produce no impact whatsoever upon the furious J. A. Pettifer.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0014 }

“Is it trouble? May my soul be blessed, I would certainly imagine there is sufficient trouble. Miss, the problem lies in the fact that I discovered your aunt’s Jersey cow inside my oats once more, under thirty minutes back. Pay attention, as this makes three times. I caught her there on Tuesday of last week and I caught her there the day before today. I traveled to this place and informed your aunt to ensure it did not happen another time. She permitted it to happen another time. Miss, where can your aunt be found? I merely wish to locate her for a brief moment and speak bluntly to her . . . speak as J. A. Pettifer bluntly speaks, miss.”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0015 }

“Should you be referring to Miss Thirza Abernethy, my aunt she is not, and her departure to East Welby was to visit a far-off relation of hers who is exceedingly sick,” stated Nell, her loftiness growing appropriately alongside each utterance. “It causes me much regret that my oats should have been trespassed upon by my cow . . . my cow she is, rather than Miss Abernethy’s . . . three years back, when she was a small calf after he purchased her from Mr. Bell, Obed presented her to me.”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0016 }

“Apologies, young lady! Expressing regret will not fix what happened. You ought to walk over and view the destruction that creature caused among my oats . . . crushed them completely from the middle to the edges, young lady.”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0017 }

“I am very sorry,” reiterated Nell resolutely, “but maybe Dolly would not have entered had you maintained your fences more effectively. The section of the boundary fence dividing your oatfield from our pasture belongs to you, and I observed just a few days ago that its state was quite poor.”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0018 }

“There is nothing wrong with my fence,” Mr. Pettifer retorted, his fury escalating at this offensive maneuver into his own territory. “A demonic cow of that sort could not be contained even by the prison fence. Furthermore, you ginger-haired slip of a thing, if that cow belongs to you, as you claim, your time would be far better spent keeping her away from the grain of others instead of lounging about reading yellow-backed books,” . . . casting a contemptuous look at the blameless tan Virgil near the feet of Nell.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0019 }

A thing other than Nell’s hair was red right then . . . a feature that had forever been a sensitive subject for her.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0020 }

“I’d prefer to possess red hair instead of being completely hairless, apart from a small strip encircling my ears,” she snapped.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0021 }

The strike struck home, because Mr. Pettifer was actually extremely touchy regarding his hairless scalp. His fury gagged him once more and left him able only to stare wordlessly at Nell, who regained her composure and pressed her upper hand.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0022 }

“Because I possess an imagination, I am able to excuse you, Mr. Pettifer. It is simple for me to picture how extremely aggravating discovering a cow among your oats must be, and the remarks you made will not cause me to hold a grudge against you. That Dolly will not ever force her way into your oats again is something I promise you. On that matter, I pledge my word of honor.”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0023 }

“Well, take care that she does not,” murmured Mr. Pettifer with a rather hushed voice; nevertheless, he marched away in quite a rage, and Nell listened to his self-directed muttering until he moved beyond her hearing.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0024 }

With a deeply troubled spirit, Nell strode across the yard and locked the mischievous Jersey inside the milking pen.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0025 }

“Unless she pulls down the fence, getting out of there is impossible for her,” she mused. “At present, she appears quite calm. It is likely that those oats have made her feel ill. Selling her to Mr. Shearer when he expressed interest last week would have been better, I wish I had done so, yet I considered it preferable to hold off until the stock auction took place and dispose of the lot as one. The claim that Mr. Pettifer is a crank seems to be accurate. He definitely shares no kindred spirit with anyone.”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0026 }

Nell constantly kept an alert watch to spot matching souls.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0027 }

Thirza Abernethy pulled into the yard just as Nell emerged from the house, prompting the latter to rush inside and prepare tea. As they sat at the tea table, the issue was discussed between them.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0028 }

“I will be happy once the sale is finished,” Thirza remarked. “Holding such a large amount of livestock around the property with only that untrustworthy Martin to care for them creates too great a burden. He has failed to return so far, despite promising he would definitely return yesterday evening if I granted him the day to attend the funeral of his aunt. I certainly have no idea how many aunts belong to him. Since he was employed here twelve months back, that makes four who have passed away. Once the harvest is gathered and Mr. Pembroke assumes control of the farm, I will be deeply grateful. Until Martin arrives, we must confine Dolly to the enclosure, because she needs to be placed in the rear field and those boundaries require repair. Truly, it amounts to a universe of grief, just as Agatha states. Over there, poor Mary Farrow is on her deathbed, and whatever will happen to her pair of youngsters is beyond my understanding. A brother of hers resides in British Columbia and she has sent a letter to him regarding them, though no response from him has reached her yet.”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0029 }

“What manner of children are they? What ages have they reached?”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0030 }

“Six minutes after . . . a pair of twins.”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0031 }

“Oh, ever since the time Mrs. Rudge gave birth to so many, I’ve had a particular fascination with twins,” Nell said enthusiastically. “Are they good-looking?”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0032 }

“Gracious, it was impossible to see . . . their filth was so great. Robin was outside creating mud pies when Lucy stepped out to bring him back inside. Robin shoved her face-down into the largest pie, and after she wept, he climbed in too and rolled around to demonstrate that no tears were necessary. Mary mentioned that Lucy actually behaved quite well, whereas Robin possessed a mischievous nature. It could be argued he was never raised properly. Shortly after his birth, his father passed away, and Mary’s poor health has persisted virtually from that moment on.”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0033 }

“Children who are raised without guidance always make me feel pity,” Nell remarked with gravity. “As you are aware, I possessed none until you began taking care of me. It is my hope that they will be cared for by their uncle. Precisely how is Mrs. Farrow related to you?”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0034 }

“Mary? Absolutely none. It was her spouse . . . he was related to us as a third cousin. Mrs. Sowerby is walking across the yard now. I figured she would come up to get news concerning Mary.”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0035 }

“Please do not inform her regarding Mr. Pettifer and the cow,” begged Nell.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0036 }

Thirza gave her word, although there was really no need for it, because Mrs. Sowerby had barely settled into her seat when she remarked,
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0037 }

“While I was returning from Delford today, Mr. Pettifer was seen by me driving your Jersey from his oats. It appeared to me that he was quite furious. Was a big fuss made by him?”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0038 }

Nell and Thirza secretly traded entertained grins. Scarcely anything in Brierley ever went unnoticed by Mrs. Sowerby. Just that morning Nell had remarked,
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0039 }

“Should you retire to your personal chamber when night turns to twelve, turn the key in the lock, lower the window shade, and let out a sneeze, the following day Mrs. Sowerby would inquire about the state of your cold!”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0040 }

“I think he did,” Thirza confessed. “I wasn’t there. He told Nell what he thought of her.”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0041 }

“I believe he is an extremely unpleasant individual,” declared Nell, indignantly throwing back her reddish head.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0042 }

“You have never spoken a more accurate word,” Mrs. Agatha stated with gravity. “I was certain that difficulty would arise the moment Robert Bell disposed of his property to an individual from New Brunswick, indeed I was. I cannot imagine what Brierley is turning into, given that such a multitude of unfamiliar folks is flooding inside it. Before long, resting peacefully in our beds will no longer be secure.”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0043 }

“Why, what different visitors are arriving here?” Thirza asked.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0044 }

“Are you unaware? To begin with, there is a Trask family. The former home of Peter Mott has been leased by them. That man was engaged by Peter to operate his mill. Coming from down east, they are complete unknowns to everyone. Additionally, the Timothy Cotton family, who are lazy, plan to relocate from Pale Sands, becoming nothing less than a strain on the community. He suffers from consumption . . . whenever he is not committing theft . . . while his wife is a spiritless woman incapable of performing any task. Sitting down is how she does her dishes. An orphaned nephew of her husband, Anthony Tulk, has been taken in by Mrs. Laurence Tulk. He will be attending your school, Nell, which means you should anticipate difficulty, mark my words. Furthermore, an additional new student will be yours. Arriving from the States, Cedric Stanhope will reside with his grandmother. Thirza, do you recall his father . . . Stephen Stanhope, the one who abandoned Rosalind Penrose over in Welby?”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0045 }

“I am not of the opinion that she was jilted by him. A quarrel took place . . . it seems to me that both parties shared the fault.”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0046 }

“At any rate, he never wed her, and rumor has it she has been extremely odd ever since . . . residing entirely alone in that small stone dwelling named Echo Cottage. Stephen departed for the States, entered into a enterprise with his uncle, and took a Yankee as his wife. He has not returned home a single time, even though his mother has traveled up to visit him on one or two occasions. His wife passed away two years ago, and he is dispatching the boy back home to his mother for a time. He is ten years of age, and I am uncertain whether he will prove to be a very pleasant student. It is impossible to know what to expect from those Yankees.”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0047 }

Mrs Sowerby viewed everyone who possessed the bad luck of being born or raised anywhere other than St. Brendan’s Island with an unequivocal can-any-good-thing-come-out-of-Nazareth attitude. It was possible, naturally, that they were decent individuals; nevertheless, one was wiser to remain skeptical. A particular bias against “Yankees” was harbored by her. A Boston boss for whom her husband had formerly labored had defrauded him of ten dollars, and no angels, principalities, or powers possessed the ability to persuade Mrs. Agatha that the entire United States did not bear the blame for this.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0048 }

“A bit of fresh blood will do Brierley school no harm,” Thirza remarked drily, “and provided this youth resembles his father, he will do fine. Steve Stanhope was the finest boy ever brought up around here, even if certain folks considered him arrogant. I imagine Mrs. Stanhope will be delighted to take the youngster in. Ever since her husband passed away, she has been terribly lonely.”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0049 }

“Well, the boy might be fine, but he will not resemble Brierley children,” stated Mrs. Agatha, as though that settled the issue. The views held by Mrs. Agatha regarding any individual, location, or item were invariably durable. “What is this rumor about you beginning a Village Improvement Society, Nell?”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0050 }

“I was merely discussing it with a few of the girls and boys during the recent Debating Club,” Nell stated, her face reddening. “They believed it would be quite pleasant . . . as do Mr. and Mrs. Wace. Many villages possess them these days.”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0051 }

“Indeed, a world of trouble awaits you if you proceed. It would be wiser to drop the matter, Nell, truly. Nobody enjoys being made better.”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0052 }

“Oh, we do not intend to attempt the betterment of the populace. It is Brierley on its own. A great deal could be performed to render it more attractive. To give an example, would it not be a change for the better if Mr. Levi Gammon could be persuaded by us to demolish that terrible aged dwelling situated on his upper farm?”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0053 }

“It certainly would,” Mrs. Agatha conceded. “For years, the settlement has had its view spoiled by that old ruin. However, if your group of Improvers manages to persuade Levi Gammon into performing an unpaid act for the community, I hope to witness the sight and sound of it myself, that’s what. I am not trying to dishearten you, Nell, because your notion might hold value, even if you likely derived it from a trashy American periodical; nevertheless, managing your school will keep you completely occupied, so my friendly counsel is to leave these improvements alone, that’s what. Even so, I realize you will proceed once your determination is fixed. You have constantly been someone who manages to complete a task one way or another.”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0054 }

The definite contours of Nell’s lips indicated that Mrs. Agatha was quite accurate in her judgment. Nell had set her heart on creating the Improvement Society. Hugh Carrow, who would be instructing in Pale Sands yet was bound to return home every Friday evening until Monday morning, showed great enthusiasm for the project; furthermore, the majority of the other people were ready to join any endeavor that involved periodic gatherings and thus a bit of “fun.” Regarding the nature of these “improvements,” no one possessed a very distinct concept apart from Nell and Hugh. The pair had discussed and mapped them out to such an extent that a perfect Brierley lived within their imaginations, even if it was found nowhere else.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0055 }

Mrs. Agatha possessed a further piece of information.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0056 }

“A Honora Hollis has been assigned the Delford school. Nell, weren’t you at Regent’s alongside a girl by that name?”
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0057 }

“Indeed, yes. Honora instructing at Delford! How utterly delightful!” cried Nell, her grey eyes brightening so much that they resembled stars in the night sky, making Mrs. Sowerby ponder once more if she would ever resolve to her own contentment whether Nell Harcourt was actually a lovely girl or if she was not.
{: #nw-v02-c01-p0058 }
